claims.claim: Decision making is the action or process of thinking through possible options and selecting one; the working definition in this lesson is attributed to OpenStax's Principles of Management (section 2.1).

Managers at every level of an organization make decisions, and those decisions affect stakeholders — everyone the organization touches, from customers and employees to suppliers and owners; a good decision can help a business thrive while a poor one can push it toward failure.

The rational decision process runs: recognize that a decision is needed, generate multiple alternatives, analyze the alternatives, select one, implement it, and evaluate its effectiveness; this lesson restates that spine in plain language as define the problem, gather information, weigh options, choose, act, and review.

Programmed decisions are repeated over time and can be guided by an existing set of rules because their criteria are known or can be estimated, and they can run on heuristics — mental shortcuts that produce an adequate solution quickly; nonprogrammed decisions are novel and unstructured, with criteria that are not well defined and information that is often ambiguous or incomplete, requiring judgment and creative thinking.

Anchoring (an initial reference point pulling later judgments toward it) and confirmation bias (favoring information that supports existing beliefs and downplaying information that challenges them) are among the barriers that degrade the quality of decision making.

Anchoring is a cognitive bias in which the first piece of information offered — typically a number or reference point — serves as an anchor that later judgments stay close to, so people's estimates are pulled toward the initial value.

Bounded rationality is the idea that decision makers cannot be fully rational because they cannot grasp every possible alternative or every implication of each one; the concept is associated with Herbert Simon, whom Britannica calls an influential proponent, and Simon also promoted satisficing — choosing the first acceptable option — and won the 1978 Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences for his pioneering research into the decision-making process within economic organizations.

Group decisions bring more knowledge and perspectives, generate more options, let individual biases cancel out, and raise commitment among participants, but they are slower, can bog down in conflict, and can fall into groupthink — members suppressing dissent to keep the peace — so agreement alone is not evidence of a good decision; remedies include diverse membership, encouraging everyone to speak, and a devil's advocate.

Because time and information are limited (bounded rationality), a good decision process raises the odds of a good outcome but cannot guarantee it; the honest habit is to review the outcome and change course when reality disagrees — a framing this lesson states explicitly as its own synthesis, grounded in bounded rationality and the evaluation step of the process.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How many steps the decision process has
positions: OpenStax (section 2.5) presents six steps: recognize that a decision is needed, generate multiple alternatives, analyze the alternatives, select one, implement it, and evaluate its effectiveness.
Some textbooks compress the process to four or five steps (e.g., merging analysis and selection), while others split evaluation into monitoring and adjusting.

This lesson uses a six-step plain-language version — define the problem, gather information, weigh options, choose, act, and review — that keeps the spine of the OpenStax model and maps one-to-one onto it.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: No substantive conflict: all versions agree the process starts by recognizing a problem, generates and compares alternatives, commits to one, and checks the result. The step counts differ only by granularity, and the lesson states its restatement explicitly as a plain-language version of OpenStax's six steps.

positions: OpenStax (section 2.4) lists anchoring among the barriers to effective decision making that managers should recognize and counter.
Investopedia treats anchoring as a cognitive bias in its own right — the tendency for a first reference point to pull later judgments toward it.
This lesson names anchoring as a decision trap, uses the Investopedia definition, and notes that the psychology subject owns the bias in depth.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Complementary, not conflicting: OpenStax groups anchoring with other barriers at the managerial level, Investopedia defines the underlying bias, and the lesson draws on both without contradicting either.
